label: Factoring Quadratics & Polynomials
overview: Factoring rewrites an expression as a product, making it easy to find zeros or simplify. On the SAT, factoring quadratics is the fastest route to solving ax²+bx+c = 0 — quicker than the quadratic formula for most problems. You also need to recognize difference of squares and GCF factoring.

keyFormulas.name: Standard quadratic (a=1)
keyFormulas.latex: x^2 + bx + c = (x + p)(x + q) \text{ where } p+q=b,\ pq=c

steps.title: Find two numbers
steps.content: Need two numbers that multiply to 12 and add to −7. Those numbers are −3 and −4.

steps.title: Write the factored form
steps.content: Replace the trinomial with two binomial factors.

steps.title: Apply zero-product property
steps.content: If a product equals zero, at least one factor is zero.

steps.title: Apply difference of squares
steps.content: x² − 9 = x² − 3² fits the pattern a² − b².

commonMistakes.fix: Check both conditions: the product pq equals c (watch the sign of c!) and the sum p+q equals b.

commonMistakes.mistake: Skipping the GCF step before factoring the quadratic
commonMistakes.fix: Always factor out the greatest common factor first. It simplifies the remaining trinomial and can change the leading coefficient.

commonMistakes.mistake: Stopping at the factored form without solving for x
commonMistakes.fix: If the question asks for solutions (roots/zeros), set each factor equal to zero and solve.

quickTip: Check your factoring by expanding: (x+p)(x+q) should equal the original trinomial. This takes 10 seconds and catches sign errors.
